questions.prompt: You cold-call a prospect and they pick up sounding rushed, one-word answers immediately. You:

options.text: Push through your opener exactly as planned.
Speed up your pitch to get the key point in before they hang up.
Ask if now's a bad time and offer to catch them at a better one.
Name it: "Sounds like I've caught you mid-something — better time to call back?"

questions.prompt: A gatekeeper says the decision-maker "isn't available" for the third call in a row. What's really going on is usually:

options.text: They genuinely have a packed calendar.
You need a different angle to get past the gatekeeper next time.
You haven't yet given the gatekeeper a reason to let you through.
Ask the gatekeeper directly what would make this worth passing on.

questions.prompt: You're 15 minutes into a first meeting with a senior prospect. They've been checking their phone repeatedly. What do you do?

options.text: Keep going, faster, before you lose them.
Stop and ask if there's something urgent they need to handle.
Call it out lightly: "I can come back another time if this isn't working."
Name what you're seeing: "Looks like something else is pulling at you, what's going on?"

questions.prompt: Your champion has gone quiet for 10 days after a strong meeting. Most likely explanation?

options.text: They're busy, they'll come back when ready.
Something internal has shifted: priorities, politics, or budget.
They've gone cold, time to escalate to their manager.
They didn't have the authority they implied, and the real decision-maker said no.

questions.prompt: A prospect says, "Let me think about it." What does that usually mean?

options.text: They need more time to weigh it up.
They have an unspoken objection they don't want to raise here.
They're being polite and the answer is no.
Someone else in the room has veto power and hasn't said so yet.

questions.prompt: You're in a meeting with three stakeholders. The most senior person is silent the whole time. What's your read?

options.text: They're delegating, they trust their team.
They're watching how their team interacts with you.
They're disengaged and the deal is in trouble.
They're the actual decision-maker and the team is performing for them.

questions.prompt: Mid-pitch, a prospect crosses their arms and leans back. You:

options.text: Carry on, body language doesn't always mean what people think.
Slow down and check in: "Am I tracking with what matters to you?"
Switch to a different angle to re-engage them.
Name it: "I get the sense something I just said landed differently than I intended."

questions.prompt: You're prepping for a meeting with a CFO. What do you focus on understanding before you walk in?

options.text: The product features most relevant to finance.
The CFO's current pressures: board reporting, cost discipline, cash position.
What ammunition the CFO needs to push back on the project internally.
Where the CFO sits politically: ally, blocker, or neutral.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes how you read a buyer's true priority?

options.text: Ask them directly what's most important.
Listen for what they keep returning to, even when the conversation moves on.
Watch what they push back on hardest, that's usually closest to the truth.
Notice what they say versus how they say it, and where the two don't match.

questions.prompt: A prospect tells you they have "no budget." Most experienced sellers know this usually means:

options.text: Exactly what they said, the budget doesn't exist.
Budget exists, but this isn't a priority yet.
Budget exists, but they don't yet trust the ROI.
Budget exists somewhere, but they don't have the authority to release it.

questions.prompt: You've made nine dials this morning and had four hang-ups. Dial ten, your internal state is:

options.text: Numb to it now — you stopped feeling the rejections a while back.
You push the next dial out faster, trying to outrun the feeling.
Curious about what's different about the calls that don't hang up.
Aware your energy has dropped, and you consciously reset before dialing.

questions.prompt: A prospect hangs up on you mid-sentence. Your first internal reaction is:

options.text: You shrug it off completely, zero reflection, straight to the next number.
You call straight back to finish your point.
You wonder whether timing, not your pitch, was the real issue.
You name it honestly to yourself — "that stung" — then dial again, clear-headed.

questions.prompt: Your manager gives you blunt critical feedback in a 1:1. Your first internal reaction:

options.text: Defensive, you start mentally building counter-arguments.
You take it in quietly and process it later.
You push back on the spot to test their reasoning.
You name what you're feeling: "That stings, give me a second."

questions.prompt: A prospect raises their voice at you in a meeting. You:

options.text: Match their energy to show you're not intimidated.
Stay quiet and let them finish, then respond calmly.
Apologise to de-escalate, even if you don't fully agree.
Name it: "Something's clearly hit a nerve, talk me through it."

questions.prompt: You can feel yourself getting defensive mid-negotiation. The most useful move is:

options.text: Push through, don't show weakness.
Ask a question to buy yourself thinking time.
Acknowledge it openly: "I notice I'm pushing back hard, let me slow down."
Reframe the conversation back to their goals.

questions.prompt: Your biggest deal of the quarter just went to a competitor. The first 24 hours you:

options.text: Get straight back on the phones, momentum is everything.
Take some quiet time to process before reaching out to anyone.
Run a structured post-mortem: what could you have done differently.
Sit with the disappointment, then debrief honestly with your manager.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes credit for an idea you brought to the team. You:

options.text: Let it slide, the work matters more than the credit.
Note it, watch the pattern, decide what to do next time.
Confront them directly after the meeting.
Raise it cleanly: "Hey, that was actually my idea, I'd like the next one to land properly."

questions.prompt: A client has cancelled on you three times in a row. Internally you feel:

options.text: Frustrated, you start considering whether they're worth chasing.
Curious about what's really going on for them.
Anxious, worried the deal is slipping.
Aware that the pattern itself is the data, time to address it.

questions.prompt: You're in a slump. Three weeks, no closes. Your dominant self-talk is:

options.text: "Push harder, more activity will fix this."
"What am I missing? What's the pattern in the losses?"
"I'll come good, slumps end."
"I'm feeling the pressure, that itself is affecting how I'm showing up."

questions.prompt: Your manager assigns you a difficult account with a reputation for chewing up reps. You:

options.text: Accept it and quietly worry whether you're being set up to fail.
Take it as a chance to learn something hard.
See it as a chance to prove yourself.
Ask your manager directly what success looks like and what support is available.

questions.prompt: A prospect says "we're all set, not interested" within your first five seconds on the phone. You:

options.text: Say thanks for your time and hang up — respect the no.
Jump straight into your value proposition to change their mind.
Ask one short question before you let them go.
Name it: "Totally fair — most people say that before they've heard why I called. Thirty seconds?"

questions.prompt: A prospect answers, hears three words, and snaps "Take us off this list" before hanging up. On your very next dial, you:

options.text: Soften your opener defensively, bracing for another rejection.
Dial faster and push harder to make up the momentum.
Take a breath and open exactly as planned, unchanged.
Notice the flinch, name it internally, and reset your tone on purpose before the next hello.

questions.prompt: It's 3 days from quarter-end and you're 40% short of target. Your default move:

options.text: Activity, activity, activity. More calls, more emails, hammer the pipe.
Triage the pipeline ruthlessly, focus only on what can actually close.
Pick up the phone to your strongest relationships and ask plainly.
Step back for an hour to think before acting.

questions.prompt: Mid-demo, the platform crashes. In front of the buying committee. You:

options.text: Apologise profusely and try to reboot.
Acknowledge it, make a light joke, switch to a backup explanation.
Name it: "Not the demo gods today, here's what you would have seen."
Stay calm, suggest a follow-up demo, and use the time to ask more discovery questions.

questions.prompt: A prospect blindsides you with a technical question you genuinely can't answer. You:

options.text: Try to answer it anyway and risk being wrong.
"That's a great question" while you stall.
Say honestly: "I don't know, but I'll find out and come back to you today."
Redirect: "Before I answer that, help me understand why it matters in your context."

questions.prompt: A deal you thought was locked has gone silent after a verbal yes. Three days. You:

options.text: Send a chase email asking for an update.
Wait it out a few more days, don't seem desperate.
Pick up the phone and call directly, no more email.
Call and name it: "I sense something's shifted, what's changed since we last spoke?"

questions.prompt: You're in a meeting and the most senior person is openly hostile. The other attendees go silent. You:

options.text: Try to win the senior person over by agreeing with their concerns.
Hold your position politely and let the data speak.
Push back directly: "I think we see this differently, can we work through it?"
Name it: "I can see this isn't landing the way I'd hoped, what would be useful to dig into?"

questions.prompt: It's Monday morning. Your first 10 cold calls have been brutal. Call 11, you:

options.text: Take a 5-minute break, reset, then dial.
Dial with exactly the same energy as call 1.
Push through, the law of averages will turn.
Notice your tone has slipped, recalibrate consciously, then dial.

questions.prompt: Your boss tells you a key account is moving to a competitor. Effective immediately. Your first reaction:

options.text: Argue the decision, push to keep the account.
Accept it cleanly and ask what you can learn from the loss.
Ask to do a final exit conversation with the client.
Sit with the hit, then debrief with your boss properly.

questions.prompt: You have roughly seven seconds after "hello" before a cold prospect decides whether to keep listening. You use them to:

options.text: State your name and company clearly.
Ask if they have a minute to talk.
Reference something specific about their business to earn the right to continue.
Open with one line tied to something specific happening in their world right now — not your pitch.

questions.prompt: First 60 seconds with a brand-new prospect. The most effective opening is:

options.text: A clear summary of who you are and what you do.
A relevant insight about their industry that earns the next 5 minutes.
A provocative question that challenges their assumptions.
A short, specific story about a similar client and the problem you solved.

questions.prompt: You need to explain a technically complex feature to a non-technical buyer. You:

options.text: Walk them through it step by step at a simplified level.
Use an analogy from a world they already understand.
Skip the how and focus only on the business outcome.
Tell a story about a customer who had the same gap and what changed.

questions.prompt: Following up after a no. The best message is:

options.text: A polite thank-you and a request to stay in touch.
An article or insight relevant to the reason they declined.
A direct question: "Help me understand what would need to be different next time."
A short story about a buyer who said no, then came back 6 months later, and what changed.

questions.prompt: You're the third quote on the prospect's desk. They've heard the same pitch twice already. You:

options.text: Differentiate on price or terms.
Differentiate on service, support, or relationship.
Lead with a story or insight the other two won't have shared.
Name the situation: "You've probably heard versions of this twice already, here's what I think the other two will have missed."

questions.prompt: A prospect pushes back hard on your pricing. The strongest response is:

options.text: Walk them through the value calculation logically.
Hold the price, explain that quality has a cost.
Tell the story of a buyer who picked the cheaper option and the cost of that choice.
Ask what they're comparing it to, and explore the gap.

questions.prompt: You stumble mid-pitch. Lose your thread completely in front of the prospect. You:

options.text: Push through and hope they didn't notice.
Pause, apologise, restart the section.
Make a light joke, acknowledge it, keep going.
Name it cleanly: "I just lost my thread, let me come back to the point that actually matters."

questions.prompt: The single most important moment in a closing conversation is:

options.text: The pricing reveal.
The silence after you've asked for the business.
The handling of the final objection.
The moment you name what's actually being decided: "This isn't really about X, is it."

questions.prompt: You're using a customer case study in a pitch. The most powerful version of it:

options.text: Numbers and metrics: percentage improvements, dollar value.
The before/after transformation of the customer's situation.
The specific moment the customer realised they had the problem.
The human behind the result: who they were, what they were afraid of, what changed.
